candidates.title: Install and secure one NVIDIA DGX A100 rack rail
candidates.objective: Orient the correct left or right DGX A100 rail, support and level it across the rack depth, depress the front metal tab, align and insert both spring-loaded prongs into the designated front-post holes, extend the rail to the matching rear rack unit, insert both rear prongs, verify full spring extension, and secure the rail using the specified bottom-hole screws.
skills: bimanual support and regrasping of a long rigid rail
simultaneous tab depression and two-prong hole alignment
maintaining level alignment across separated rack posts
rear telescoping adjustment without losing front engagement
Phillips-driver alignment and controlled screw fastening
candidates.success_conditions: The correct rail is installed at the designated rack unit through robot-applied forces only; both front and rear pairs of prongs occupy their intended holes; each retaining spring is fully extended; front and rear attachments are at the same rack unit; the rail supports itself after release; and the required screws occupy the bottom holes while the reserved top holes remain empty. The final state must persist for 3 seconds after the robot releases the rail and tool. Score zero for a wrong-side or reversed rail, mismatched rack units, partial or false prong engagement, use of the reserved top holes, dropped hardware, permanent rack/rail deformation, or teleporting, welding, or state overwrite. Partial credit may separately recognize correct orientation, front retention, level rear alignment, rear retention, and correct screw placement. Component physics must pass unsupported retention, spring-return, telescoping, screw-thread, wrong-hole, and overload controls before a robot demo.
candidates.industrial_value: NVIDIA's DGX A100 service manual defines this as installation of the server rack-mount kit and states that the kit acts as the shelf supporting the system. It is therefore a real data-center installation operation, not generic object placement. The procedure requires correct rack-unit registration and complete spring-prong engagement before the heavy server can be mounted.
candidates.dexterity: High but feasible with rigid PhysX. A robot must control a long, asymmetric articulated rail with separated contact sites, depress a retaining tab while inserting two spring-loaded prongs, preserve the first attachment while extending and aligning the rear, and then change to a screwdriver grasp. The defining capability is staged, load-bearing mechanical latching across two rack posts, not connector mating or simple pick-and-place.

candidates.asset_plan: Independently model a square-hole rack segment and one DGX A100 rail from the manual's depicted geometry and measurements from legally obtained reference hardware; do not redistribute NVIDIA manual media or an unlicensed mesh. Use rigid links for the rail body and telescoping section, prismatic joints for extension, and articulated rigid tab/prong/spring proxies calibrated from hardware. Preserve the actual two-prong pattern, rack-hole pitch, handedness markings, front/rear interfaces, bottom screw holes, and reserved top chassis holes. First validate collision clearances, tab travel, spring return, full/partial insertion discrimination, front retention during extension, rear rack-unit alignment, screw capture, load-bearing stability, and reset repeatability. Only after those tests pass should the task be connected to pinned Isaac Sim 6.1.0 and YAM commit 0059d02a1a91bc6834c1d0846022891df0c78730. The robot must manipulate every task object through contacts; static rack anchoring is allowed, but the rail and fasteners may not be teleported or dynamically welded.
candidates.risk: Medium implementation risk. The acquired manual establishes the sequence and engagement checks but does not provide rail CAD, prong spring constants, thread dimensions, allowable insertion force, or damage limits. Those properties require reference-part measurement, and no numerical force threshold should be claimed beforehand. The acquired benchmark catalogs include rack-adjacent operations such as pressing a cable into a clip and tightening a thumbscrew, but no objective combining handed long-rail handling, spring-prong latching at two posts, rack-unit leveling, and prescribed screw-hole use was found. That screen is not proof against every accepted, pending, open, or team submission; selection remains conditional on a complete synchronized semantic review before implementation and again after completion.

candidates.title: Release and remove a Lenovo ThinkSystem SR590 hot-swap fan
candidates.objective: With the documented service access already established and hazardous fan motion absent, press the fan-cage bracket toward the server front, maintain the release, grasp the top of the specified system fan, and lift it vertically from its bay without disturbing neighboring fans or the cage.
skills: bimanual coordination between latch release and extraction
top grasp on a closely packed module
force control that preserves the cage and fan housing
candidates.success_conditions: The designated fan is removed vertically by robot contact after the cage bracket is moved toward the front; it is placed stably in the service area; the cage, neighboring fans, and bay guides remain seated and undamaged. The final state must persist for 3 seconds. Score zero for removing the wrong fan, lifting before release, contacting a moving rotor, displacing another fan, dropping the module, damaging the cage, or changing object state without robot action. Partial credit may distinguish correct bracket actuation, secure fan grasp, and partial guide-controlled withdrawal. Development must remain blocked until the exact latch dependency and bay geometry are verified on reference hardware.
candidates.industrial_value: Lenovo explicitly identifies the part as a hot-swap fan and says removal can avoid significant interruption to system operation. That establishes a real availability-sensitive data-center maintenance operation.
candidates.dexterity: Moderate. The task couples a directional cage-bracket release with a constrained lift in a crowded server interior. It is more meaningful than free pick-and-place, though less demanding than the selected rail task because the source specifies only a short two-action sequence and does not establish a complex regrasp or fastening phase.

candidates.asset_plan: Model the SR590 fan bay, cage bracket, neighboring fan envelopes, guide surfaces, and removable fan as rigid bodies using the official figure plus measurements from matching hardware. Represent the bracket/latch with an articulated joint and calibrated retention, not a scripted release. Validate that an unreleased fan remains retained, correct bracket motion permits vertical extraction, neighboring modules remain constrained, and reset restores retention. A full YAM scene should be attempted only after these tests pass in the pinned runtime.
candidates.risk: Not selected. The acquired source does not provide dimensions, latch travel, retention forces, or an explicit statement that bracket pressure must be maintained during lifting. The hot-swap wording also creates a safety ambiguity: although the manual permits powered service, a robot demo should use a stationary de-energized fan unless an equipment-specific safe powered test is separately justified. Its short release-and-lift skill overlaps broadly with existing latched-module removal tasks and offers weaker novelty than the rail objective.

candidates.title: Install a tool-less Open Rack V3 IT support bracket from inside the frame
candidates.objective: Orient one Open Rack V3 IT support bracket inside the rack, align its tool-less mounting features with the specified frame cutouts, engage and lock the bracket without external access, and leave it seated without interfering with adjacent brackets or chassis space.
skills: bimanual support of an elongated load-bearing part
clearance management around adjacent rack hardware
candidates.success_conditions: Blocked pending the referenced OCP CAD/drawing and a concrete bracket design. At minimum, a valid rubric would require all documented tool-less mounting features to be engaged from inside the frame, correct OpenU registration, self-support after release, no interference with nearby brackets or chassis envelopes, and no permanent deformation. No hook count, insertion motion, latch state, force threshold, or success claim may be invented from the currently acquired text.
candidates.industrial_value: The Open Rack Meta Frame V3 specification defines these brackets as the shelf support for IT gear, requires tool-less direct mounting, inside-frame serviceability, and substantial load capacity. This establishes industrial relevance, but not yet an executable manipulation sequence.
candidates.dexterity: Potentially high because a long load-bearing bracket must be registered and latched within a constrained rack interior. The exact dexterity cannot be asserted until the referenced bracket CAD and drawing reveal its real mounting features.

candidates.asset_plan: Do not begin task construction from the prose alone. First obtain the exact OCP collateral named in section 12.8, confirm its license, select one bracket revision, and extract its mounting-feature geometry and rack interface without mixing revisions. Then build an independent rigid PhysX model, validate every engagement feature, incorrect-level rejection, self-support, adjacent-clearance, overload behavior, and reset repeatability before considering YAM integration.
candidates.risk: Blocked and not selected. The acquired specification proves purpose, access direction, tool-less mounting, and load requirements, but the referenced CAD/drawing is not present in the acquired package. The actual hooks, tabs, latches, insertion trajectory, dimensions, and retention mechanics are therefore unknown. Treating this as build-ready would require invented geometry and success criteria; it may also be semantically close to other rack-rail or shelf-support installation tasks.

selection_reason: The DGX A100 rail objective is the strongest valid non-connector candidate. It has an official manufacturer procedure with explicit orientation, rack-unit alignment, spring-prong insertion, visible engagement checks, rear extension, prescribed fastening, and a prohibited screw-hole choice. These constraints support a rigid-body task that tests bimanual long-part handling, compliant latching, maintained alignment, regrasping, and tool use. The SR590 fan objective is industrially real but shorter, safety-sensitive, and more similar to generic latched-module removal. The OCP bracket objective has strong industrial importance but is blocked because its defining mounting geometry is only referenced, not acquired. Selection is conditional: rail geometry, spring and thread behavior, damage limits, YAM reachability, and the complete accepted/pending/open/team novelty comparison remain unverified, so no demo or submission success is asserted.
